name: Psalms

objectives.text: Identify the Psalms as songs and prayers that God's people sang to the Lord
Recite Psalm 23:1 and tell one thing it says about God as a shepherd
Name David as the shepherd and king who wrote many of the psalms
Describe how the psalm writers prayed to God both in times of joy and in times of sorrow
Explain what Psalm 19 teaches about the heavens declaring the glory of God
Classify a psalm as praise, thanksgiving, or lament by pointing to words and features in the text
Explain the contrast between the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked in Psalm 1
Describe how a psalm title links the psalm to an event in David's life, such as Psalm 51 and David's sin with Bathsheba
Explain how Christians have used the Psalms as a pattern for their own prayers
Analyze a lament psalm by identifying its address to God, complaint, petition, statement of trust, and vow of praise
Compose a written prayer in class that follows the structure of a praise, thanksgiving, or lament psalm
Compare Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 and explain how together they introduce the themes of the whole Psalter
Explain what the images of God as rock, refuge, fortress, and shepherd teach about his character
Explain what Psalm 119 teaches about the word of God and describe its acrostic structure
Analyze synonymous, antithetic, and synthetic parallelism in lines of Hebrew poetry
Describe the five-book division of the Psalter, locate the doxology that closes each book, and explain the traditional comparison with the five books of Moses
Explain the setting of the Songs of Ascents as songs of pilgrimage to worship in Jerusalem
Summarize how the historical psalms retell Israel's story to teach the next generation God's faithfulness and Israel's failures
Explain what the penitential psalms teach about sin, confession, and God's forgiveness as the Reformed tradition confesses repentance
Interpret the Messianic psalms by tracing how the New Testament applies them to the suffering and reign of Christ
Explain the possible meanings of Selah and other musical terms in the superscriptions and why scholars remain uncertain about them
Compose an original psalm in a chosen genre that uses Hebrew parallelism and the genre's typical structure
Trace the movement of the Psalter from lament toward praise across its five books, ending in the closing Hallelujah psalms
Analyze how the Psalms bring the full range of human emotion before God and explain the Reformed teaching that they model honest prayer
Evaluate major interpretive approaches to the imprecatory psalms in light of God's justice and the New Testament teaching on vengeance
Defend the singing of psalms in corporate worship from Scripture and the confessions, and compare exclusive psalmody with the use of hymns within Reformed churches
Produce a study of the kingship of the Lord in the enthronement psalms and its fulfillment in the reign of Christ

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (songs to God, David as writer, Psalm 23, joy and sorrow, genres, prayer with Psalms, Psalm 1 and 2, parallelism, Messianic psalms, five books, Selah, emotions, imprecatory psalms, corporate worship, kingship of the Lord). Replaced 'Apply a Psalm to your own feelings' with observable composition tasks. Recast the 'theology of the emotions' objective as an analysis of the text and the tradition's teaching. Added psalm imagery, Psalm 19 and creation, Psalm 119 and acrostics, psalm titles and David's history, lament structure, Songs of Ascents, historical psalms, penitential psalms, and the lament-to-praise shape of the Psalter. Anchored each objective to specific verses. Kept WCF 8.4 for the Messianic psalms and added confessional references only where they state the doctrine, including WCF 21.5, WSC Q87, Q98, and Q26, Heidelberg Q117, and Belgic Article 2.
